Search continues for 22 after bulk carrier sinks off India
item.description:
India’s Coast Guard and Navy continued search-and-rescue operations off the eastern coast on Sunday after a Panama-flagged cargo vessel carrying 24 crew sank, with two Chinese nationals rescued, a senior official said.

The two rescued Chinese seafarers said the vessel developed a list on Friday and sank within eight minutes, forcing crew to abandon ship, Shyam Jagannathan, director general of India’s Maritime Administration, told Reuters.

Jagannathan said the chances of finding survivors generally fall sharply after 12 hours, but rescuers were continuing the search.

Twenty-two crew members remain missing from the Ocean Winner, including 18 Chinese nationals, three Myanmar nationals and one Bangladeshi, according to the Indian Coast Guard.

The Indian Navy is closely coordinating with the Coast Guard to locate the remaining crew, the Navy said in a post on X.

The Coast Guard has sent two vessels from Sri Vijaya Puram, formerly known as Port Blair, for the search-and-rescue operation, a Coast Guard spokesperson said.

The Ocean Winner was carrying iron ore bound for China after departing from India’s eastern Paradip port on Friday, according to an initial report prepared by India’s Maritime Administration.

The cargo ship sank about 240 nautical miles from the port, according to government sources. The cause of the sinking was not immediately known.

item.title: Starc heroics see Australia thrash Bangladesh in second Test
item.description:
An irrepressible Mitchell Starc bagged four wickets and 10 for the match as he ripped through the Bangladesh batting to ensure a commanding innings and 51-run second Test victory for Australia inside two days on Sunday.

The visitors headed into the Mackay showdown on a high after shocking the world’s top-ranked team by nine wickets in the first Test at Darwin.

But they were brought crashing back to earth by some scintillating fast bowling, led by Starc who finished with 10-51 for the match to level the two-game series.

After 18 wickets fell on a frenetic first day in Mackay, the hosts were all out for 210 in the morning session, securing a lead of 146 on the back of Cameron Green’s 67.

Star Bangladesh quick Shoriful Islam claimed 7-48 — the best figures from a Bangladeshi bowler in an away Test.

The visitors crashed for just 64 in their first innings, when Starc took 6-12, and he was the chief tormentor again, claiming 4-39 while Pat Cummins took 3-10 and Nathan Lyon 3-25.

Bangladesh had a horror start with Shadman Islam lasting just three balls, playing a nothing stroke to a moving Starc delivery and edging to Marnus Labuschagne at point.

Mominul Haque was equally clueless next ball, failing to offer a shot with Starc removing his off stump and setting up a hat-trick opportunity.

Captain Najmul Hossain Shanto, who was out for a golden duck in the first innings, this time survived to deny Starc.

But their woes deepened when Tanzid Hasan departed soon after for nine.

Starc was again involved, taking a catch in the deep after Tanzid pulled Cummins.

Shanto did well to soak up the pressure after lunch for 46 deliveries, but he eventually lost focus against the off-spin of Nathan Lyon, holing out to the safe hands of Starc at long off on 31.

And when Starc was brought back into the attack, he was front and centre again, enticing a loose shot from Litton Das who was caught without scoring by Beau Webster at third slip.

Mehidy Hasan Miraz struggled to get going and departed to an equally poor shot, lashing at a Cummins bouncer and collected by wicketkeeper Alex Carey.

The Australian captain then removed Hasan Mahmud (two) before Starc took his 10th for the match — the fourth time he has achieved the feat — when he bowled Taijul Islam for seven.

Lyon quickly wrapped up the tail in the first over after tea.

Australia resumed at 165-8 with Green on 51 and Lyon on 10.

Green, who scored a century during the first Test in Darwin, kept the scoreboard moving early with quick singles.

But he was undone by an inswinging yorker from the impressive Shoriful that hit him on the toe with a review declaring him out lbw.

A valiant Lyon brought up the 200 for Australia with a towering six off Taskin and with Josh Hazlewood adding 24 crucial runs for the last wicket.

The innings ended when Hazlewood skied Taijul to Shadman on six to leave Lyon not out 32.

item.title: Iran warns any country joining US sanctions considered “enemy”
item.description:
Iran on Saturday warned countries against participating in the United States' "economic war" against the Islamic republic, saying they would be considered enemies.

Washington has pushed its allies to jump aboard Donald Trump's new campaign to isolate the Iranian economy, as the US President's unpopular war drags toward the six-month mark.

"We declare to all countries... do not join the economic war waged by the United States," said Mohsen Rezai, the head of Iran's supreme national security council, on state television.

"Any country participating in the imposition of economic restrictions against us is considered an enemy," he added.

If the countries concerned refused to "distance themselves" from the United States, Iran would "harm" their interests, he added.

Rezai also insisted that the Islamic republic had more cards to play in the war, claiming that "we have not yet attacked any American economic interests".

"So far, we have only targeted military bases, but if they want to impose economic sanctions on us, the United States has oil and economic companies around Iran and elsewhere, and we will strike them," Rezai threatened.

Should Trump "take action, our confrontation will be like an earthquake", he added.

Washington has also called on other governments to join its efforts to isolate the Iranian economy, notably Beijing, among Iran's top strategic partners.

But China has criticised the initiative, arguing that American sanctions would not resolve the conflict in the Middle East.

One of Iran's major trading partners, the United Arab Emirates, announced on Tuesday that it was suspending all trade and financial transactions with Tehran until further notice.

LGRD minister: Local govt elections to be held on time
item.description:
Local government elections will be held on time by strictly following constitutional procedures and rules, newly appointed Local Government, Rural Development and Cooperatives Minister Dr Abdul Moyeen Khan said on Sunday.
“Elections would be held at all five tiers of local government, with the government expecting genuine representatives of the people to be elected,” he said.
The minister made the remarks while exchanging views with officials of the ministry and its subordinate agencies at the Secretariat on his first working day after assuming office.
Asked when local government elections would begin and whether they would be completed within a year, Moyeen Khan said there was a constitutional process for holding the elections and that it would not be appropriate for him to announce a specific date without following that process.
“Following the constitutional process and observing all the rules, the BNP government will announce the local government elections at the appropriate time,” he said.
The minister said holding local government elections within a particular timeframe was not his personal target but a government objective aimed at reflecting the will of the people.
He stressed that local government elections were not limited to city corporations.
“There are elections at different tiers of local government. Elections will be held at all five tiers, and our expectation is that genuine representatives of the people will be elected,” he said.
Noting that the elections of 2008, 2014, 2018 and 2024 had failed to reflect the will of the people, the minister said he considered the February 12, 2026 election an opportunity through which genuine representatives of the people had come before the country.
The minister also described the Local Government, Rural Development and Cooperatives Ministry as different from many other ministries because of its direct and day-to-day engagement with citizens.
“The main objective of the government is to serve the people, and this ministry is among those that work directly with the people every day, 365 days a year,” he said.
Moyeen Khan said local government was an important component of the democratic system and that the effective functioning of the ministry would contribute to the overall functioning of the government and the country.
He said the ministry worked directly with people at the grassroots and pledged to ensure that government policies and services reached them effectively.
The minister said the government would succeed when services were properly delivered to people at the grassroots.
He said the government would serve all citizens, but special attention would be given to poor, disadvantaged and underprivileged people.
“Those who are affluent and wealthy are less dependent on government support because they can manage many of their own needs. But poor people need greater assistance from the government,” he said.
According to estimates, around 40 percent of Bangladesh’s population still lives in poverty in one form or another, he said, adding that the rights of poor people had been deprived during the previous government. He also highlighted the Family Card and Farmer Card programs introduced by BNP Chairman Tarique Rahman.
He said his focus would remain on addressing the needs of disadvantaged people and that he wanted to work alongside citizens, standing with them, to serve the country under the responsibility entrusted to him by the prime minister.

North Sea oil, once the driving force of the UK economy, may be dwindling but it remains a symbol of prestige and a rich resource for political debate

When oil was first discovered off the north-east coast of Scotland in September 1969, industry folklore has it that the duty superintendent on the rig carefully poured it into a pickle jar commandeered from the canteen and took it back to Amoco’s Great Yarmouth office in Norfolk. There, it was emptied into an ash tray, sniffed and then set alight.

From that modest start, North Sea oil – as the huge basin of oil and gas reserves quickly became known – emerged as a driving force of the British economy and a symbol of national power and renewal as the UK emerged from the Opec oil crisis.

item.title: Pakistan to host South Asian Games in April next year
item.description:
ISLAMABAD: Pakistan will host the South Asian Games from April 3 to 11 next year, 23 years after it last staged the regional sports gala in Islamabad in 2004.

The decision was taken at a meeting of the Executive Committee of the South Asia Olympic Council held here on Sunday, with Pakistan Olympic Association (POA) president Arif Saeed, who is also president of the South Asian Olympic Committee, in the chair.

The meeting reviewed preparations for the Games and approved three host cities — Islamabad, Lahore and Peshawar.

Representatives from Bangladesh, Maldives, Nepal and Sri Lanka attended the meeting in person, while India participated through video link. All the representatives endorsed the proposed dates, according to sources.

A visiting delegation is scheduled to inspect proposed sporting venues in Islamabad on Monday.

The Games will feature 28 sports and 346 medal events, with more than 3,200 athletes expected to participate across the three host cities. A large number of technical officials will also be part of the event, with Pakistan preparing to host around 4,000 athletes and other foreign visitors.

During Sunday’s meeting, representatives of the participating countries reviewed preparations and measures being taken by Pakistan to host the regional event.

The federal government has already given the go-ahead to the POA and other stakeholders to hold the Games and announced that the required funds would be released.

Pakistan was originally scheduled to host the Games in 2021, but the event was subsequently postponed for various reasons. Preparations are now said to be in their final stages.

The visiting delegation also visited the Taxila Museum and other historical sites on Sunday.

Sources said the Capital Development Authority (CDA), on the direction of the federal government, had started preparations to provide accommodation and other facilities to foreign visitors arriving in Islamabad next year for the South Asian Games and other international events, including the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) conference.

“The federal government has been taking every possible step to make the three international events next year in Islamabad highly successful — the South Asian Games, SCO conference and a meeting of the OIC,” a senior government official told Dawn.

He said the POA, Foreign Office and federal government were monitoring preparations to ensure that the Games were hosted successfully.

“Everyone is on board and working as a team for these Games,” he said.

Asked about India’s participation, the official said its representative had joined Sunday’s meeting through video link and endorsed the dates, which, according to him, indicated that India intended to participate.

However, another source cautioned that India’s participation could not yet be confirmed.

“India has been mixing politics with sports and has avoided visiting Pakistan. Even recently, it did not participate in a volleyball event,” the source said.

item.title: New govt pay structure: Delay in decision will complicate situation: Debapriya Bhattacharya
item.description:
Debapriya Bhattacharya, distinguished fellow of the Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD) and convener of the Citizen’s Platform for SDG Implementation, believes the government lacks the political courage to introduce a new pay structure for government employees.

He said keeping the issue pending will not reduce the problem; rather, the situation will become more complicated the longer the government delays taking a decision.

Debapriya Bhattacharya made the remarks at a media dialogue organised by CPD on the government’s six-month performance at CPD’s office in the capital’s Dhanmondi on Monday.

CPD’s another distinguished fellow Mustafizur Rahman and additional research director Toufiq-ul Islam Khan were also present.

Debapriya Bhattacharya said, “Even after six months, you have not been able to take a decision on pay and allowances. Why can’t you? There is a major issue, which is financial capacity. There will be a shortfall of Tk 1.4 trillion from the revenue collection target of Tk 6.95 trillion for the current fiscal year.”

Debapriya Bhattacharya further said, “The interim government had left a report on the pay structure, and after evaluating it, a recommendation was made to implement the pay structure in phases, which everyone had also agreed to. Instead of delaying so much, if you had initially provided a 20–25 per cent dearness allowance and asked for some time, that would have been very good. The situation has now been brought to a point that is not good.”

Debapriya Bhattacharya believes keeping the issue pending will not reduce the problem; rather, the situation will become more complicated the longer the government delays. According to him, delays in taking a decision on pay and allowances will also disrupt the government’s other activities.

62,000 people lost jobs

Regarding the government’s six-month performance, CPD said 95 factories in the country’s three major industrial zones have permanently closed between January and August this year. As a result, 61,881 people have lost their jobs.

Debapriya Bhattacharya said the government inherited some structural difficulties when it took office. The global situation was also not favourable at the time. War broke out. The problem is that the government did not prepare a comprehensive document on the situation it inherited when it assumed responsibility. As a result, it is now difficult to assess various measures and economic progress, he said.

He said the government has repeatedly stated that it took charge amid a difficult situation. But no comprehensive, data-based document was prepared on the situation from which the government took responsibility. As a result, it has now become difficult to reconcile the government’s various statements with statistics, he said.

Mentioning that there were two major expectations from the new government—economic recovery and establishing good governance—Debapriya Bhattacharya said some discomfort has emerged in these areas.

No comprehensive action plan has been seen for the reform programme. Many of the commissions mentioned in the manifesto have also not been implemented, he added.

Debapriya said CPD has prepared a list of around 362 measures to assess the new government’s promises and various steps it has taken. These have been divided into nine categories and are being evaluated under the 'Reform Tracker'.

For good governance, 105 incidents have been included in the assessment. The decision by government MPs not to take plots and cars, the speedy trial of the Ramisa murder case and the initiative to bring discipline to the transport system using artificial intelligence were mentioned as positive measures.

On the other hand, CPD considers the appointment of politically affiliated individuals to senior positions a matter of concern. Debapriya also said the government has deviated from its commitment to making appointments based on merit.

item.title: Reopening border haats, lifting restrictions on yarn imports discussed with Indian envoy
item.description:
Bangladesh’s Commerce Minister Khandakar Abdul Muktadir and Indian High Commissioner Dinesh Trivedi discussed several issues aimed at further strengthening trade relations between Bangladesh and India.

According to a statement from the Commerce Ministry, the two sides discussed reopening the border haats that have remained closed, making the land ports fully operational and lifting restrictions on the import of yarn through land routes.

The issues were discussed at a meeting between Commerce Minister Khandakar Abdul Muktadir and Indian High Commissioner Dinesh Trivedi at the Secretariat on Monday.

The meeting also covered expanding bilateral trade, removing trade barriers, promoting joint investment and increasing cooperation between businesses of the two countries.

After the meeting, the commerce minister said bilateral trade between Bangladesh and India currently stands at around USD 13 billion. However, trade has slowed somewhat over the past one and a half years due to various obstacles. The meeting focused on identifying these problems and discussing ways to make trade easier and more effective.

The commerce minister said India is Bangladesh’s second-largest trading partner after China and that the two countries have longstanding economic ties.

He said priority was given to bringing the land ports into full operation, reopening closed border haats and lifting restrictions on yarn imports by land to further strengthen economic relations.

The minister also said a proposal had been made to form a joint task force to enhance cooperation between businesses in the two countries.

The two sides also discussed creating new investment opportunities and making business communication easier through improvements in digital infrastructure.

Indian High Commissioner Dinesh Trivedi said that although Bangladesh and India have some differences on political and economic issues, their people want development and progress. The two countries need to work together, particularly for the future of their younger generations, he said.

Trivedi also said Bangladesh and India are independent and sovereign countries. Neither country is bigger or smaller than the other, and both are equal. Relations should move forward on the basis of this equality, he said.

The Indian high commissioner said economic cooperation is the most important factor in improving relations between the two countries. In his view, stronger economic ties would create opportunities for cooperation in other areas as well.

Emphasising joint investment and production, Trivedi said Bangladesh’s garment industry has been successful in global markets. India could support the sector by supplying zippers, machinery, buttons and other inputs, he said. This would further increase mutual dependence between the two countries.

Praising Bangladesh’s garments, he said he feels proud when he sees clothing labelled “Made in Bangladesh” in international markets. The country’s garment sector could expand further through joint initiatives between Bangladesh and India, he added.

The meeting also placed emphasis on increasing cooperation between businesses, creating new investment opportunities and strengthening supply chains. Both sides expressed hope that these initiatives would further strengthen trade relations between Bangladesh and India.

Cabinet approves draft Armed Police Battalions Act, 2026
item.description:
By UNB

The cabinet on Monday approved the draft of Armed Police Battalions Act, 2026, with a view to modernising and making the force more people-friendly by abolishing the existing ordinance.

The approval came from the cabinet meeting chaired by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman at the Secretariat.

According to the proposed law, the Armed Police Battalion will be entrusted with responsibilities, including maintaining public security, providing security to VIPs and government-declared important installations, and taking action against those involved in terrorism, drug trafficking, human trafficking, rape and crimes against humanity.

The battalion, which is part of the police force, will also assist other law enforcement agencies in maintaining law and order.

The draft law also proposes empowering the members of the battalion to investigate criminal offences and conduct related proceedings, subject to compliance with the Code of Criminal Procedure and other laws.

It further proposes provisions for the establishment of special courts and summary courts and lays down procedures for conducting trials.

Under the proposed law, the Armed Police Battalion will operate under the control and supervision of an additional inspector general of police.

The draft law was prepared in Bangla, making the existing legal framework more up-to-date and the Armed Police Battalion more people-oriented.

The draft was uploaded on the website of the Ministry of Home Affairs to seek public opinion.

The proposed law seeks to repeal the Armed Police Battalions Ordinance, 1979, but retains the validity of actions taken under the existing ordinance.

The draft law was given final approval by the Cabinet subject to vetting by the Legislative and Parliamentary Affairs Division.

For decades, Hong Kong mourned when the mainland could not. Its huge annual Tiananmen vigil kept alive the memory of the 1989 pro-reform protests in Beijing, and of the massacre that suppressed them. item.title: The Guardian view on Britain helping Ukraine: build the weapons independence Kyiv needs | Editorial
item.description:
Moscow hopes western politics will weaken support for Kyiv. The UK and Europe’s answer should be to make Ukraine increasingly capable of defending itself alone

The events of the past few days on Europe’s borders may mark a turning point in Russia’s war on Ukraine. While the political skies in Kyiv have darkened for Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the military picture looks brighter. Ukraine can already send swarms of drones against Russian oil facilities, e-commerce warehouses and airfields. Andy Burnham’s arrival in Kyiv marks a step forward. Britain is releasing classified information on its components of Scalp, the French version of the Anglo-French Storm Shadow cruise missile, enabling its assembly in Ukraine. This is more than another weapon for Kyiv. Britain is helping Ukraine become less dependent on the western armoury.

Moscow sabre-rattles, but Britain should hold its nerve. Kyiv has been at the mercy of its allies, waiting to replenish weapons stockpiles and release sophisticated arms. Producing its own hi-tech armoury gives Ukraine greater freedom of action because western governments have let go. Two years ago it was different. Joe Biden waited until November 2024 before letting Ukraine strike deep into Russia with US weapons. Yet thresholds once deemed dangerously escalatory have since been crossed without provoking a Russia-Nato war. Kyiv is now being trusted with something more consequential: a measure of weapons independence.

item.title: Trump can huff & puff but without political fix Iran won't come down
item.description:
The latest U.S. strategy in the Middle East is defined as one of “maximum pressure,” combining military containment and economic sanctions in an attempt to compel Iran to accept a deal. But it lacks clearly defined, civilian-led outcomes, illustrating the persistent misalignment between military means and political ends.

Military pressure can set conditions, signal resolve, and buy time for civilian action. It cannot determine political outcomes. When a civilian-led strategy rooted in clear end states is not determined ahead of sending military forces, those deployments turn into continuous rotations; it is how ‘forever wars’ get started.

This essay is not an argument against the use of force. It is at times necessary, and even realist restraint doctrine says so. Instead, this essay is an argument that force is but one of many instruments of national security; when the other instruments of national security, like diplomacy, aren’t employed equally or greater than the military, it is service members who pay the greatest price.

An earlier article laid the framework for this argument; this article shows what the habit of overreliance on the military looks like in practice. It is about what happens when whole-of-government strategic planning doesn’t take place before the first bullet is fired – leading to strategic failure even if the military objective is achieved.

On March 4, 2026, U.S. Army Vice Chief of Staff General LaNeve testified that more than 108,000 U.S. Army soldiers only (not counting military forces from the other services) were deployed or forwardly postured across 160 countries. Many, more than 50,000 personnel from all the services, are deployed to the U.S. Central Command area of interest in the Middle East. They include sailors still at sea aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln. These forces have frequently been deployed to display U.S. resolve or apply “pressure” but have remained overseas longer than they or others anticipated.

Legendary deterrence theorist Thomas Schelling described a difference between using force to physically destroy an adversary's capability and using force as a threat to change an adversary's behavior. The former is a military task; the latter is a political strategy, effective only if a settlement is feasible. According to Schelling, "the power to hurt is bargaining power." But when pressure is applied without the possibility of a political settlement, force is all that remains.

In the 1991 Gulf War, the U.S. military stopped after liberating Kuwait and declined to advance to Baghdad. The political and military leadership (of President George H.W. Bush and Gens. Colin Powell and Norman Schwarzkopf, Jr.) agreed that continuing to Baghdad would trade a decisive military victory for an open-ended occupation for which the country wasn’t prepared. That was a wise political decision made before forces were committed.

Twelve years later, the U.S. political leadership ordered an invasion of Iraq without first answering the question of who would pick up the pieces after the military had done its job. While postwar civilian authorities were established, they were deployed too late, and post-conflict planning failed to assign civilian responsibilities and resources for security beyond military control. What was missing was the whole-of-government strategy on the who, what, where, when, and how the desired political outcome was to be achieved.

"You are going to be the proud owner of 25 million people,” then-Secretary of State Powell warned President George W. Bush before the invasion. “You will own all their hopes, aspirations, and problems. You'll own it all.” His warning, later dubbed the Pottery Barn rule — “if you break it, you own it” — underlined the importance of allocating responsibility for planning for the “day after” the use of force. The answer must always be America’s elected civilian leadership, not the uniformed members of the military; answers to the “who, what, where” questions must be known before forces are committed, not afterwards.

In Afghanistan, the military removed the regime and won on the battlefield. But multiple U.S. administrations failed to answer what specific, achievable, and time-bound political outcomes the fighting was designed to achieve. Instead, drawdown plans were based on optimistic assumptions and insufficient preparation for a full withdrawal. So when the political decision was finally made to bring the troops home and abandon Kabul in 2021, it was done in a hurried and improvisational manner, turning the operation into an evacuation, on the fly and under fire.

The 2026 Iran war has followed a similar pattern. On February 28, U.S. and Israeli aircraft struck Iran, opening the current phase of the conflict. While the military achieved its tactical objectives, there was no clearly defined civilian-led strategy to achieve the publicly stated political goal of overthrowing the Iranian regime, or at least forcing it to make significant concessions. An interim agreement established a 60-day negotiating period for a final agreement and temporarily paused military operations, but, without a clear political strategy, this had little hope of succeeding.

The result has been a return to violence as both sides claim to control, or even own, the Strait of Hormuz. U.S. forces are once again deployed to the Middle East with no end in sight. What started as a military pressure campaign to first destroy nuclear-related infrastructure and then remove the regime — something pressure alone (particularly air pressure only) can never achieve — has turned into the longest ever deployment of a U.S. aircraft carrier at sea without a port call and another “forever” conflict.

Ordering the deployment of forces is easy, but disengagement and redeployment are hard work. Powell used eight questions, and former Defense Secretary Casper Weinberger set down six criteria, including requirements that combat be a last resort and objectives be clearly defined before commitment. Which model used doesn’t matter so much as adhering to a model. It’s the discipline to not get into a fight without an exit strategy.

This touches on one reason the military is repeatedly asked to accomplish strategic outcomes beyond its mandate. Unlike other government institutions, the military teaches strategy and planning, and at scale. It has dedicated masters degree-granting institutions and dedicated career fields, such as the U.S. Army’s Functional Area 59 (Strategist). In contrast, the Department of State has genuine expertise, and its foreign service officers execute complex diplomatic missions every day, but it lacks a year-long, in-residence, career-gated strategist program; so does every other major agency that make up the other elements of national security.

The fix is for the president and Congress to build civilian capacity, tied to career advancement, to the same degrees the military currently possesses. Then, when national leadership convenes the government’s national security experts to consider the use of force, it is the civilian strategist who must be heard in at least equal measure as the military planner.

Unfortunately, when the government equates military pressure to strategy, it asks military forces to do the work that would be far more appropriately assigned to their political, diplomatic, or development counterparts. Military forces are designed to close with and destroy the enemy, not negotiate or oversee political settlements.

Deploying teams into high-risk environments and getting them home safely is common operational preparation. Every unit that deploys does it. Every combatant command does it. What is missing is the same preparation at the level above the uniform, from the civilian political leadership appointed over the military. Before you send them, know how, and when, you bring them back. Anything less is not strategy. It is the beginning of another long deployment.
